name: Belarusian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War
watch: Belarus's most-visited museum, in the 2014 'Victory' building. Belstat counted 196,700 visitors in 2020, a Covid year.
records_note: A state museum under the Ministry of Culture; lists only administrators, not a board.
affiliations_note: Has two branches: the Old Border military historical complex and the memorial complex to internationalist servicemen.

propaganda.summary: Founded 1944. The government built its new premises as its central politics of remembrance project, opened 2 July 2014 by Lukashenko and Putin. The exhibition keeps the Soviet heroic narrative of the war.

overview: National war museum at 8 Prospekt Pobediteley, Minsk, beside the "Minsk, Hero City" stela in the Pobeda (Victory) museum-park complex (stated by the museum).

Opened in October 1944 in Minsk soon after its liberation. Wikipedia gives 25 October 1944 and says the collection began in November 1942. It moved in 1966, in 1977 and to its current building in 2014 (Wikipedia).

The current building opened on 2 July 2014 (Minsk tourism portal), with the Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko and the Russian president Vladimir Putin attending (Wikipedia; Attractions Management). The architects call its form an "architectural salute", and a dome houses the Victory Hall (Minsk tourism portal).

The museum states 10 exhibition halls covering 4,200 m² with over 8,000 exhibition items, and about 30 collections of more than 155,000 storage units, including photographs, documents, letters and personal belongings of war participants.
Wikipedia calls it the most visited museum in Belarus and gives about 234,900 visitors in 2012.
Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 19:00, closed Monday. Ticket office closes at 18:30. On-site parking and a site version for visually impaired users.
details.funding_verdict: Belarusian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War: a Belarusian state museum
funding: The museum's site titles it «Учреждение «Белорусский государственный музей истории Великой Отечественной войны»», in English an institution, the Belarusian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War (translation). Wikipedia names it the Belarusian State Great Patriotic War Museum.
The 2014 building was opened by the heads of state of Belarus and Russia, Lukashenko and Putin, together with war veterans (Attractions Management, 8 July 2014).
details.bottom_line: The museum names itself a Belarusian state institution, and the presidents of Belarus and Russia opened its current building in 2014. Those two facts are the documented link between the museum and state leadership.

name: National Centre for Contemporary Arts
watch: State body formed 1 Oct 2015. Director Siarhei Kryshtapovich, in post since 2018, was commissioner of Belarus's last official Venice pavilion, 'Exit' (2019).
records_note: A state-budget body being liquidated under a 3 August 2026 resolution.
affiliations_note: Formed in 2015 by merging the Museum of Contemporary Fine Arts with the Creative Workshops; its premises and collections pass to the National Art Museum and the Academy of Arts.

overview: State art centre in Minsk with two venues: a Stalinist-style building at Prospekt Nezavisimosti 47 and a building at Nekrasova Street 3, built for artists in the early 1980s, with 940.7 square metres of exhibition space in total (Russian Wikipedia).

Established on 1 October 2015 by a Council of Ministers resolution (Russian Wikipedia gives that date in its text and cites a decree of 10 August 2015, no. 673, in its links), merging the Museum of Modern Fine Arts (1997 to 2015) and the Creative Workshops Centre of Contemporary Arts (2011 to 2015). It answers to the Ministry of Culture (Russian Wikipedia).
The predecessor Creative Workshops were founded by Mikhail Savitsky, who offered three-year residencies to artists. After his death in 2010 the workshops closed in 2011 (Russian Wikipedia).
Collection of 4,936 works by 892 Belarusian and foreign artists from the 20th and early 21st centuries (Russian Wikipedia).
Directors: Natalya Sharangovich (2015 to 2017) and Sergei Krishtapovich (2018 to 2025) (Russian Wikipedia).

It ran exhibitions, education, research and international cooperation, took part in special projects at the Venice Biennale in 2015 and 2017 and organised the Minsk Triennial (Russian Wikipedia). Nasha Niva adds that it supported experimental projects in visual, theatre and music art, worked with young artists and curators and took part in international projects including Belarus's national pavilions at the Venice Biennale. Charter97 says it organised the national pavilions at three Venice Biennales.

Closure: the centre announced that exhibitions at Nekrasova Street 3 would stop from 22 June 2026 (Nasha Niva, 4 May 2026). The Council of Ministers agreed to liquidate it. The resolution was published on the national legal portal on 5 August 2026 and liquidation is to finish by 30 November 2026. The last exhibition closed on 2 August, and about 50 employees lose their jobs (Charter97, 5 August 2026).

Charter97 reports, from two unnamed sources, that the collections and the Yakub Kolas Street site pass to the National Art Museum and the Nekrasova Street building to the Belarusian State Academy of Arts.

Unverified: Charter97, an opposition outlet, writes that some link the closure to Andrei Vasilevsky, the new head of the Artists' Union and the Academy's vice-rector for administrative work, and that social media users link it to the renovation of the National Art Museum and the construction of a new Academy building.
details.funding_verdict: National Centre for Contemporary Arts: state-funded: Belarus state budget through the Ministry of Culture
funding: The centre was created by a Council of Ministers resolution and answers to the Ministry of Culture (Russian Wikipedia).
On liquidation, the Council of Ministers directed the centre's unused budget funds to the Belarusian State Academy of Arts and the National Art Museum (Charter97, 5 August 2026).
details.bottom_line: The money behind the centre is the Belarusian state budget, and the state that created it has now ordered it liquidated by 30 November 2026, with its unused funds passing to the Academy of Arts and the National Art Museum.

name: Argos
watch: Structural support comes from the Flemish Community ministry and the Flemish Community Commission. The City of Brussels and Flemish Audiovisual Funds back projects.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Lists its seven-person board but posts no annual report or accounts and names only the Flemish Government as funder.

overview: Centre for audiovisual arts at Werfstraat 13 (rue du Chantier), 1000 Brussels, in the Les Quais district (argos website).

Founded in 1989 in Brussels to stimulate and promote Belgian audiovisual arts. It began with screenings in cultural centres across Belgium and soon distributed videos to festivals, art institutions and television networks abroad (argos, "Our history").
Founding directors were Koen Van Daele (1989 to 1993) and Frie Depraetere (1989 to 2013). Niels Van Tomme directed it from December 2018 to February 2024 (argos, "Our history").
Building: since 1999 it has occupied a former storage facility, after several moves around the city (argos, "Our history").

On site: two exhibition spaces, a projection room, a media library, a climate-controlled archive, studios, offices, a cafe and a bookshop. The collection holds more than 5,000 artist films and videos (argos, "Our history").

Visiting: open Thursday to Sunday, 11:00 to 18:00. Visitors choose their contribution: 10 euros recommended, 5 euros for visitors with less to spend, 15 euros to give extra support. Entry is free for under-18s, ICOM members, Museumpass holders, visitors with disabilities and their assistant, and press. Paspartoe holders and Article 27 visitors pay a reduced price, with Article 27 at 1.25 euros (argos, "Visit us").
details.funding_verdict: Argos: mainly public: the Flemish Government
funding: The site states "argos is supported by the Flemish Government"; since 1994 argos has been primarily subsidised by the Flemish Community (argos, "Our history").

Board (argos, "Our team"): presidents Mohanad Yaqubi and Jens Van Lathem; members Anouk De Clercq, Kristof Van Hoorde, Tom Bonte, Sorana Munsya and Dirk De Wit. Joachim Naudts is general and artistic coordinator.
details.bottom_line: The money behind argos is public: the Flemish Community has been its main subsidy provider since 1994, and the Flemish Government is its only named funder. Worth watching is its dependence on that single public funder.

name: Braemhuis (Renaat Braem Huis)
funding: Herita vzw, a heritage non-profit, runs it with the City of Antwerp. The Flemish Government set EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year under a one-year agreement.
watch: Renaat Braem left the house to the Flemish Community in 1999. Herita has worked since 2024 to open it to the public.
records_note: Herita lists its 11 board members and 17 sites on its site, and the Flemish Government announces its funding decisions on vlaanderen.be.
finances_note: Flemish Government figure of EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year (decision of 13 December 2024). No figure for the Braemhuis alone.
affiliations_note: Run by Herita vzw, a non-profit that manages 17 heritage sites in Flanders and has been Flanders' first recognised heritage network since 1 May 2024. Member of Iconic Houses.

overview: Live-work house of the architect and planner Renaat Braem at Menegemlei 23 in Deurne, a district of Antwerp. It is named for him (Herita, Wikipedia).
Braem lived there until 1997. In 1999 the house and its contents were donated to the Flemish Government (Onroerend Erfgoed inventory).

Red brick facade over a hidden concrete skeleton, with interiors in wengé, oregon and limba wood and a black granite bathroom. Braem applied for the building permit in January 1955 and construction ran from February 1957 to early 1958 (inventory).
Protected as a monument since 3 April 1995. Restored in 2000 to 2002 by the architects Walter Slock and Willem Hulstaert, and a house museum since 2003 (inventory).
Since 2024 the non-profit Herita works with the City of Antwerp to open the house to the public and is studying its restoration needs (Herita).

Visiting: guided visits only. Expeditie De Stad vzw runs tours of 1 hour 15 minutes for 8 to 12 people at EUR 20 per person, every day during the day except Sundays and public holidays (expeditiedestad.be). The house is not accessible to wheelchair users (Flemish Architecture Institute event listing, 2024).
details.funding_verdict: Braemhuis: public bodies: the Flemish Government, which received the house in 1999, and the City of Antwerp, with the heritage non-profit Herita working to open it
funding: Braem gave the house to the Flemish Government in 1999 (inventory). The sources read do not state who owns it today.

Herita vzw works with the City of Antwerp to open the house. On 13 December 2024 the Flemish Government provided EUR 6.3 million for Herita's 2025 operating year, a one-year transitional agreement for maintenance and restoration at its sites. The decision does not name the Braemhuis (vlaanderen.be).
details.bottom_line: The only funding tied to the house is Flemish Government money for Herita's 2025 operations, which the decision does not link to the Braemhuis; no flagged funder appears, and no house-level figure or city contribution was found. Worth watching: the outcome of Herita's restoration study and who pays for any work that follows.

name: Constant (Association for Art and Media)
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Non-profit association for art, media and technology with an office at Rue du Fort 5A, Saint-Gilles, Brussels, and a studio at Chaussée de Jette 388, Koekelberg (Constant).
Founded in 1997 as an association. Its original statutes focused on supporting audiovisual media and electronic arts (Constant).

Its focus later moved to free software, feminisms, gender, copyright alternatives and networked artistic work. The 2023 to 2027 programme is called SPLINT, "Speculative, Libre, Intersectional Technologies" (Constant).

Constant Studio, rented since 2022, is a former workshop for electronic appliances with two floors of about 150 square metres. The ground floor holds residencies and workshops and the first floor is divided into 11 units used by artists, collectives and researchers (Constant).
Window installations are visible from the street at the office. The group also runs worksessions, publishes books and hosts projects such as the feminist server network ATNOFS.

Visiting: the office is open Monday to Friday, 10 am to 5 pm, and Constant asks visitors to call beforehand. All events are free. The office has a 20.5 cm entrance step and no lift, and Constant states its spaces are not yet accessible to everyone.
details.funding_verdict: Constant: publicly funded: Flemish, Francophone and Brussels authorities, with EU and foundation project grants
funding: Constant's Support page lists as supporters: the Departement Cultuur, Jeugd, Sport en Media of the Vlaamse Overheid; the Vlaamse Gemeenschapscommissie; Maribel funding via FE.BI; Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles (Arts Numériques); the Brussels-Capital Region; the Services du Gouvernement Francophone Bruxellois; the Dutch-language services of the municipality of Saint-Gilles; and Wallonie-Bruxelles International (ATNOFS, Iterations and Cqrrelations).

Project grants shown on the same page: the Creative Europe Programme of the European Union (Iterations), the European Cultural Foundation (ATNOFS, A Transversal Network of Feminist Servers), the Ville de Bruxelles (Open coil) and Innoviris (SpecXcraft).
details.bottom_line: Constant is a Brussels non-profit whose Support page lists Flemish, Francophone, Brussels and municipal public bodies, plus Creative Europe, the European Cultural Foundation and Innoviris as project funders.

name: Horta Museum
funding: The commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961. The museum's EUR 800k renewal is paid by Urban Brussels, the commune, Fonds Baillet-Latour, museum resources and an unnamed patron.
watch: Victor Horta's house and studio of 1898 to 1901, a museum since 1969. The first phase of facade and reception works ends in November 2026.
records_note: The commune of Saint-Gilles owns the buildings; the 2026 renovation funders were named in the press.
affiliations_note: Municipal museum of the commune of Saint-Gilles, part of the UNESCO-listed Major Town Houses of the Architect Victor Horta. Member of Iconic Houses.

overview: Museum in Victor Horta's former house (no. 25) and studio (no. 23) on Rue Américaine in Saint-Gilles, with its reception in the neighbouring building at no. 27, which Jules Brunfaut built around 1903 to 1904. Brussels Museums lists the address as no. 27 (Cercle Guimard, Brussels Museums).

Horta built the house and office from 1898 to 1901 and sold both in 1919. The commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961, it was classified in 1963 and opened as a museum in 1969 (Cercle Guimard).
Named for Victor Horta, and listed by UNESCO in 2000 as part of the Major Town Houses of the Architect Victor Horta (Wikipedia).
Exposed iron structure, a leaded-glass skylight, sgraffito walls, mosaic tiling and carved wood.

On site: furniture and objects by Horta and his contemporaries, documents on his life and temporary exhibitions, with offices, archives, ticketing, cloakroom and shop in no. 27, which the commune bought in 2007 (Wikipedia, Cercle Guimard).

Visiting: closed Mondays, open Tuesday to Friday 14:00 to 17:30 and Saturday and Sunday 11:00 to 17:30, free on the first Sunday of the month. Ticket prices and stair access not listed. The house stays open during the 2026 works (Brussels Museums, The Art Newspaper).
details.funding_verdict: Horta Museum: mainly public: the commune of Saint-Gilles owns and runs it, with Urban Brussels, the Fonds Baillet-Latour and an unnamed patron behind the 2026 renewal
funding: The commune bought the house in 1961, the studio in 1971 and no. 27 in 2007; the 2007 purchase cost EUR 1,250,000 plus EUR 2,150,000 for studies and works, made possible by Beliris, the cooperation body of the federal state and the Brussels-Capital Region (Cercle Guimard).

2026 renewal of EUR 800,000: VRT names Urban Brussels, the commune, the Fonds Baillet-Latour, the museum's own resources and a new patron who is not named. BX1 names no funders, and The Art Newspaper credits the commune alone.
details.bottom_line: The money is public: the commune of Saint-Gilles, Beliris and Urban Brussels, plus the Fonds Baillet-Latour and an unnamed patron for the 2026 renewal. The weak points are the sources' disagreement on who pays the EUR 800,000, the unnamed patron and the missing accounts. Worth watching: the patron's name and the second phase in 2029, which opens the garden and redevelops the studio.

name: KIOSK
records_note: Three funders appear as logos with no date; the Kunstensite vzw board of seven is named.
affiliations_note: KIOSK is run through Kunstensite vzw and tied to the School of Arts Ghent, KASK & Conservatorium, part of HOGENT.

overview: Contemporary art exhibition space at Louis Pasteurlaan 2 on the Bijloke site in Ghent, on the campus of the KASK School of Arts (e-flux directory; Ghent city visitor site).
An initiative of the non-profit Kunstensite vzw and University College Ghent's School of Arts. Its exhibition programme began in 2006 in a small glass pavilion (artlead.net).
Since 2010 it has been in the former anatomical theatre of the Clinical and Outpatient Institute, a neo-Gothic building from 1905 designed by Louis Cloquet (artlead.net; Ghent city visitor site).

The programme centres the artist, shows emerging and established artists through long development processes, and favours new productions. Since January 2021 it has also used its website for art projects (stated by KIOSK).

Team named by KIOSK: Simon Delobel (director), Sara Plantefève-Castryck (mediation, press and communication), Thomas Peeters and Sam Van Ingelgem (production managers). Kunstensite vzw is its governing board: Claudine Hellweg (chair), Lies Leliaert, Filip Rathé, Shila Anaraki, Anne-Françoise Lesuisse, Claire Stragier and Sevie Tsampalla.
Open daily 12:00 to 18:00. Entry is free (Nosbaum Reding exhibition page for the April to June 2026 show; Ghent city visitor site).
details.funding_verdict: KIOSK: public support: a university-college art school, the Flemish government and the City of Ghent (stated by KIOSK)
funding: KIOSK's Mission page lists three logos under "KIOSK is supported by:", linked to the websites of the School of Arts Ghent (schoolofartsgent.be), the Flemish government (vlaanderen.be) and the City of Ghent (stad.gent).
The School of Arts is also the co-founder of the initiative (artlead.net).
details.bottom_line: KIOSK is an initiative of the non-profit Kunstensite vzw and the School of Arts Ghent, and its Mission page lists the school, the Flemish government and the City of Ghent as its supporters. The money documented is public.

name: Proyecto mARTadero
funding: Its supporters page, dated 2019, names Misereor and Oxfam Internacional as current supporters, and Hivos, Conexión, Solidar Suiza, Cooperación Italiana and CAF as former ones.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: A cultural project in the Villa Coronilla zone of Cochabamba, in a former slaughterhouse built in 1924 and granted to NADA on a 30-year concession.

overview: Social development and arts project on Calle 27 de Agosto y Ollantay in the Villa Coronilla neighbourhood of Cochabamba, a few blocks from the city centre (mARTadero site; history page).

Housed in a former municipal slaughterhouse. After 1992 it served as a small school, a sports space and storage for public lighting and unused municipal furniture, and it deteriorated until 2004 (mARTadero history page).

In 2004 the building hosted the II Concurso Nacional Bienal de Arte Contemporáneo (CONART), co-organised with the Alcaldía of Cochabamba, which began its recovery. The competition was promoted by the Oficial Mayor de Cultura, Jenny Rivero, and by a group of artists led by Angélika Heckl and Fernando García. The NADA association began the works, and a loan of use was requested from the Concejo Municipal (mARTadero history page).
NADA generated the project and holds a 30-year concession on the building. Fundación Imagen manages it (mARTadero site; Quiénes somos page).
The site is about 2,900 square metres, with a survey of each room and a progressive recovery plan to adapt the spaces to multiple uses (mARTadero history page).

Programmes: Formarte, Residencias, Acción Urbana, a children's creativity workshop, cultural policy, an entrepreneurship incubator and a Maker Space, across performing arts, visual arts, architecture, audiovisual, literature and music (mARTadero site).
It describes its management as self-managed and assembly-based, with seven principles including innovation, research and interculturality (stated by the project, Quiénes somos page).
details.funding_verdict: Proyecto mARTadero: supporter-funded: Misereor and Oxfam International listed as current supporters, in a building held on a 30-year concession
funding: The Apoyos page lists Misereor and Oxfam International as current supporters, and Hivos, Conexión, Solidar Suiza, Cooperación Italiana and CAF as previous supporters. The page was posted on 25 February 2019.

Building: NADA holds the 30-year concession on the former slaughterhouse; the project's history page says the municipal council was asked for a loan of use in 2004 and the Alcaldía helped with the first clean-up.
details.bottom_line: The Apoyos page lists Misereor and Oxfam International as current supporters and Hivos, Conexión, Solidar Suiza, Cooperación Italiana and CAF as previous supporters; the building is held by NADA on a 30-year concession. The project states that it is self-managed.

name: Thapong Visual Arts Centre
funding: Board-run centre funded by the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Culture (P2.2M for the 2014 refit). Partners: HB Botswana (2024), BTC Foundation (2018), DTC Botswana and FNB Foundation (2014).
watch: De Beers gave P75,000 toward the 2014 refit. That is twelve years old and not a current funding line.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: News items name partners and a 2014 board chair; no reports, accounts or current board are public.

overview: Membership-based visual arts organisation in Gaborone with a gallery, studios and workshops, and an international residency programme that began in 2002 (Contemporary And).

Established in 1998 according to Contemporary And. Mmegi (2016) dates its origin earlier: the Thapong International Artists' Workshop was established in 1989, and in 1999 it set up a centre in an old building in Gaborone Village donated by the National Museum and Art Gallery.
Thapong began as an international artists' workshop programme in Botswana that grew out of the Triangle Arts Trust (Wikipedia, in its entry on the artist Ann Gollifer).
Building and site: a colonial-era house, formerly a residence for colonial officials, became the gallery. A coffee shop was built in front of it and six studios were added (Mmegi, 2014).
On site: gallery, six studios and a coffee shop.
It runs the Thapong Artist of the Year Awards (TAYA), introduced in 2004 (Mmegi, 2016).
Visiting: no opening hours, admission or accessibility information was found.
details.funding_verdict: Thapong Visual Arts Centre: mainly public and corporate: Botswana's culture ministry for the buildings, a diamond trading company and a bank foundation for the refit and awards
funding: 2013 to 2014 refit: Ministry of Youth, Sports and Culture, P1.5 million for new art studios; DTC Botswana, P654,908 for the gallery refurbishment; First National Bank Foundation, the coffee shop (Mmegi, 30 October 2013). Mmegi's July 2014 piece names the Department of Youth Sports and Culture, DTC, Plascon, Collegiums and the FNB Foundation as funders, gives no amounts for them, and reports the colonial-era building was renovated at a cost of P250 000.

Awards: the Botswana Telecommunications Corporation (BTC) Foundation worked with the centre on the BTC phonebook cover and TAYA competitions. The phonebook cover winner usually receives P50,000 including the exchange programme. In 2021 neither competition was held: the centre said its sponsors were hit by the COVID-19 pandemic, and that one sponsor, the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Culture (MYSC), did not host the President's Day competitions (Mmegi, 17 October 2021).
details.bottom_line: The money behind the centre is a mix of Botswana ministry funds and corporate sponsors (a diamond trading company, a telecoms company, a bank foundation) at amounts that were published only at the time of the 2013 refit. The weak point is that no accounts, reports or current board were found, and the centre has no site of its own. Worth watching: whether sponsors of the awards return after the 2021 pause.

name: National Museum of Cambodia
funding: The pages read did not state how the museum is funded. Returned objects came from a private collector, a UK dealer's estate and US museums, not from donors to the museum (AKP, 21 November 2025; The Star, 28 February 2026).
watch: Cambodia's main museum of Khmer antiquities, run under the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts. It has been the venue for returns of looted Khmer objects since 2024, including 296 objects from István Zelnik on 20 November 2025 and 74 objects from the Latchford estate in February 2026.

overview: The national museum of Cambodia in Phnom Penh, which hosts the ceremonies for returned objects (AKP, 21 November 2025).
The pages read do not state who founded it or when it opened.

What is there: returns it has received include 296 objects from István Zelnik, among them 183 Khmer silk textiles and Pre-Angkor and Angkor stone and bronze (AKP, 21 November 2025); 74 objects from the Latchford estate, including large sandstone sculptures, to join the collection (The Star, 28 February 2026); and a life-sized statue of Dhrishtadyumna from Koh Ker reunited with its pedestal in 2024 (ICIJ, 27 August 2024).
Archive: not described on the pages read.
details.funding_verdict: National Museum of Cambodia: state museum, funding not stated on the pages read
funding: No reporting found of its budget or donors in the pages read.
The Ministry thanked Zelnik for funding archaeological research at Angkor and Koh Ker and for supporting publications on Khmer heritage (AKP, 21 November 2025).

red_flags.heading: Looted or contested holdings
points: On 27 February 2026 Cambodia received 74 objects under a deal with the estate of Douglas Latchford, charged in New York in 2019 with smuggling looted relics, who died in 2020 (The Star, 28 February 2026).

ICIJ reported on 27 August 2024 that 70 artifacts were returned, at least 14 previously held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, others by Jim Clark and the George Lindemann family. Latchford's estate agreed to pay $12 million and return a 7th-century bronze statue, and Clark agreed in 2022 to return 35 relics.
On 20 November 2025 collector István Zelnik returned 296 objects at the museum. The Ministry said many were looted during the civil war (AKP, 21 November 2025).

details.bottom_line: A state museum whose funding is not published on the pages read. The story to follow is the stream of returns from Latchford-linked and other collectors.
details.website: https://www.nationalmuseum.gov.kh/ (not opened; the site address was not checked)
